The parallels with BillyElliot are unmistakable. The creators of MadeinDagenham have likewise seized on a hugely popular feelgood movie and transformed it into a big-budget, even more crowd-pleasing, British musical. But whereas Billy's personal triumphcontrastedwiththe tragic defeat ofthe miners.
For me, 'Made in Dagenham's mix of lumbering big-heartedness and wild facetiousness worked better than it had any right to do.
Rupert Goold's colourful production has more character than eight out of ten factory-built West End shows, it lacks the strict quality-control procedures that would take it from good to great.
This show, based on the 2010 film, is witty, fun, fitfully inventive and distinctly English.
As an account of a pivotal moment in women's fight for equal pay, it's a cartoonish, even juvenile version of what really happened.
But, turned into a big, brassy musical, the show has mislaid the quality that made the film so good: a real heart.
Well, apart from an amusing turn by a twinkle-toes, dancing Harold Wilson, pretty much everything [goes wrong].

There is a lot to love here, quite a bit to like and a few bits which are just wrong. But the overall impression is good.
The story has heart and I couldn’t help but get behind the characters – as honest, down to earth working mums they are immediately loveable.
A tremendous cast saves this from being yet another average new musical, with the songs mostly forgettable and some scenes plain awful.

cn.t: This British musical adaptation of the film earns praise for its heart, humor, and Gemma Arterton's performance, though critics are divided—some find it genuinely affecting and crowd-pleasing, while others dismiss it as plastic and overly sentimental.
